claim: Three-dimensional (3D) representations of the environment are often critical for selecting actions that achieve desired goals.
source: Three-dimensional (3D) representations of the environment are often critical for selecting actions that achieve desired goals.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that reflects established scientific understanding about the importance of 3D representations for goal-directed behavior.

claim: The success of goal-directed actions relies on 3D sensorimotor transformations that are experience-dependent.
source: The success of these goal-directed actions relies on 3D sensorimotor transformations that are experience-dependent.
evidence: This statement in the abstract is supported by the experimental findings presented in the manuscript showing experience-dependent associations.

claim: Neurons with more robust 3D visual representations preferentially carried choice-related activity.
source: We found that neurons with more robust 3D visual representations preferentially carried choice-related activity.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data comparing Tolerance values between neurons with and without choice-related activity.

claim: Following the onset of choice-related activity, the robustness of the 3D representations further increased for neurons with choice-related activity.
source: Following the onset of choice-related activity, the robustness of the 3D representations further increased for those neurons.
evidence: This is supported by data showing increased Tolerance values in the SPC window compared to the SD window for neurons with choice-related activity.

claim: 3D orientation and saccade direction preferences aligned, particularly for neurons with choice-related activity.
source: We additionally found that 3D orientation and saccade direction preferences aligned, particularly for neurons with choice-related activity, reflecting an experience-dependent sensorimotor association.
evidence: This is supported by data showing alignment of surface tilt and saccade direction preferences, with stronger alignment for neurons with choice-related activity.

claim: The alignment of 3D orientation and saccade direction preferences reflects an experience-dependent sensorimotor association.
source: We additionally found that 3D orientation and saccade direction preferences aligned, particularly for neurons with choice-related activity, reflecting an experience-dependent sensorimotor association.
evidence: This is supported by comparison with a previous study where monkeys were trained to report opposite stimulus features, showing that the alignment depended on task training.

claim: The parietal cortex is an important site of sensorimotor transformations.
source: The parietal cortex is an important site of sensorimotor transformations (Rushworth et al., 1997; Buneo et al., 2002; Brovelli et al., 2004; Buneo and Andersen, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Parietal lesions can result in deficits associated with the impaired use of sensory information to create and execute motor plans.
source: Parietal lesions can result in deficits associated with the impaired use of sensory information to create and execute motor plans, as opposed to deficits in sensory processing or action (Pause and Freund, 1989; Pause et al., 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on parietal lesions.

claim: Parietal lesions can produce 3D visual processing deficits.
source: However, they can also produce 3D visual processing deficits (Holmes, 1918; Holmes and Horrax, 1919).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Within parietal cortex, a major site of 3D visual processing is the caudal intraparietal (CIP) area.
source: Within parietal cortex, a major site of 3D visual processing is the caudal intraparietal (CIP) area.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on CIP function.

claim: Neurons in CIP are tuned for 3D orientation.
source: Neurons in CIP are tuned for 3D orientation (Taira et al., 2000; Rosenberg et al., 2013) signaled by multiple cues (Tsutsui et al., 2001; Tsutsui et al., 2002; Rosenberg and Angelaki, 2014b)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: CIP neurons perform multisensory processing required for gravity-centered vision.
source: and perform multisensory processing required for gravity-centered vision (Rosenberg and Angelaki, 2014a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: CIP activity correlates with the short-term memory and perceptual matching of 3D features.
source: In addition to high-level sensory representations, CIP activity correlates with the short-term memory and perceptual matching of 3D features (Tsutsui et al., 2003)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: CIP activity correlates with choices made during a binary orientation discrimination task.
source: and choices made during a binary orientation discrimination task (Elmore et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Inactivating CIP impairs 3D feature discrimination.
source: Furthermore, inactivating CIP impairs 3D feature discrimination (Tsutsui et al., 2001; Van Dromme et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: CIP projects to areas involved in motor planning and execution through eye and hand movements, including the lateral intraparietal (LIP) area, anterior intraparietal (AIP) area, and V6A.
source: In particular, CIP projects to areas involved in motor planning and execution through eye and hand movements, including the lateral intraparietal (LIP) area (Andersen et al., 1992; Bennur and Gold, 2011; Shushruth et al., 2018), anterior intraparietal (AIP) area (Murata et al., 2000; Baumann et al., 2009; Pani et al., 2014), and V6A (Fattori et al., 2010; Fattori et al., 2012; Breveglieri et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on anatomical connectivity.

claim: It is unknown if CIP neurons carry motor-related signals.
source: However, it is unknown if CIP neurons carry motor-related signals, and if so, whether they form sensorimotor associations.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: Neuronal activity was recorded while macaque monkeys performed an eight-alternative forced choice (8AFC) tilt discrimination task with planar surfaces at different slants and distances.
source: Neuronal activity was recorded while macaque monkeys performed an eight-alternative forced choice (8AFC) tilt discrimination task with planar surfaces at different slants and distances (Chang et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: The neurons differed in the extent to which their orientation tuning depended on distance.
source: The neurons differed in the extent to which their orientation tuning depended on distance.
evidence: This is supported by the Tolerance index measurements showing a range of values across neurons.

claim: Choice-related activity was preferentially carried by neurons whose 3D orientation selectivity was more tolerant to distance.
source: Choice-related activity was preferentially carried by neurons whose 3D orientation selectivity was more tolerant to distance and associated with further increases in tolerance.
evidence: This is supported by data showing higher mean Tolerance values for neurons with choice-related activity.

claim: Neuronal choice tuning was parametric.
source: Neuronal choice tuning was parametric and the choice and surface tilt preferences generally aligned.
evidence: This is supported by data showing parametric tuning curves for choice responses.

claim: The choice and surface tilt preferences generally aligned.
source: Neuronal choice tuning was parametric and the choice and surface tilt preferences generally aligned.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that the median circular difference between preferences was not significantly different from 0°.

claim: The alignment of choice and surface tilt preferences was experience dependent.
source: A comparison of results from monkeys trained to report opposite stimulus features (i.e. the near versus far side of the plane; Elmore et al., 2019) indicated that the alignment was experience dependent.
evidence: This is supported by comparison with a previous study showing that the alignment depended on task training.

claim: Many CIP neurons had saccade direction tuning.
source: Many neurons had saccade direction tuning and the saccade direction and surface tilt preferences generally aligned.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that 63% of neurons had significant saccade direction tuning.

claim: The saccade direction and surface tilt preferences generally aligned.
source: Many neurons had saccade direction tuning and the saccade direction and surface tilt preferences generally aligned.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that the median circular difference between preferences was not significantly different from 0°.

claim: The sensorimotor association between saccade direction and surface tilt preferences was strongest for neurons with choice-related activity.
source: This sensorimotor association was strongest for neurons with choice-related activity.
evidence: This is supported by data showing a narrower distribution of preference differences for neurons with choice-related activity.

claim: The coupling of sensory and motor functions at the level of single CIP neurons may facilitate sensorimotor transformations over short timescales that enable successful interactions with the 3D world.
source: The coupling of sensory and motor functions at the level of single CIP neurons may facilitate sensorimotor transformations over short timescales that enable successful interactions with the 3D world.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Two monkeys were trained to perform the 8AFC tilt discrimination task.
source: To this end, we developed an 8AFC tilt discrimination task in which the side of a viewed plane that was nearest was reported through a saccade to one of eight choice targets (Figure 1A). We then trained two monkeys to perform this task under different viewing conditions that determined the task difficulty (Chang et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes the experimental methods and is illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Planes were presented at eight tilts (0° to 315°, 45° steps).
source: Planes were presented at eight tilts (0° to 315°, 45° steps), corresponding to the eight choice options.
evidence: This describes the stimulus parameters used in the experiment.

claim: Planes were presented at five slants (0° to 60°, 15° steps).
source: Planes were presented at five slants (0° to 60°, 15° steps).
evidence: This describes the stimulus parameters used in the experiment.

claim: Planes were presented at four distances: 37, 57, 97, and 137 cm.
source: All combinations of these tilts and slants (N = 33 unique orientations) were presented at four distances: 37, 57, 97, and 137 cm (Figure 1C).
evidence: This describes the stimulus parameters used in the experiment and is illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: Behavioral and neuronal responses to 132 surface poses were measured.
source: Thus, we measured behavioral and neuronal responses to 132 surface poses.
evidence: This describes the total number of stimulus conditions tested.

claim: For both monkeys, sensitivity significantly depended on slant.
source: For both monkeys, we found that sensitivity significantly depended on slant (four-way ANOVA, both p≤6.0x10−11)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the behavioral data.

claim: For both monkeys, sensitivity significantly depended on distance.
source: and distance (both p≤1.3x10−34)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the behavioral data.

claim: For both monkeys, sensitivity did not significantly depend on tilt.
source: but not tilt (linearized into cosine and sine components, all four p≥0.21; Fisher, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the behavioral data.

claim: Sensitivity decreased with distance from fixation (57 cm).
source: Consistent with our previous findings in which performance in the 8AFC tilt discrimination task was extensively analyzed over a wider range of 3D poses and multiple visual cue conditions (Chang et al., 2020), sensitivity decreased with distance from fixation (57 cm) and increased with slant (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Sensitivity increased with slant.
source: Consistent with our previous findings in which performance in the 8AFC tilt discrimination task was extensively analyzed over a wider range of 3D poses and multiple visual cue conditions (Chang et al., 2020), sensitivity decreased with distance from fixation (57 cm) and increased with slant (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: 437 neurons were recorded from the caudal intraparietal area using laminar probes.
source: To quantify the representation of 3D surface pose in CIP while the monkeys performed the behavioral task, we recorded from 437 neurons using laminar array probes (Monkey L: N = 218; Monkey F: N = 219; Figure 2).
evidence: This describes the experimental methods and is illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: The median visual response latency was 52 ms.
source: The median visual response latency was 52 ms and the population responses to preferred and non-preferred stimuli became significantly different at 58 ms (ANOVA, p<0.05), indicating that selectivity for 3D surface pose started early in the response.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of neuronal response time courses.

claim: The population responses to preferred and non-preferred stimuli became significantly different at 58 ms.
source: The median visual response latency was 52 ms and the population responses to preferred and non-preferred stimuli became significantly different at 58 ms (ANOVA, p<0.05), indicating that selectivity for 3D surface pose started early in the response.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of neuronal responses.

claim: Selectivity for 3D surface pose started early in the response.
source: The median visual response latency was 52 ms and the population responses to preferred and non-preferred stimuli became significantly different at 58 ms (ANOVA, p<0.05), indicating that selectivity for 3D surface pose started early in the response.
evidence: This is an inference based on the timing of significant differences in responses.

claim: The onset of choice-related activity in the population response occurred at 202 ms.
source: The onset of choice-related activity in the population response followed at 202 ms (calculated in a subsequent section).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of choice-related activity time courses.

claim: The mean Tolerance during the SD window was 0.58 ± 0.15 standard deviation.
source: Across the population, the mean Tolerance was 0.58 ± 0.15 standard deviation (Std Dev; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a summary statistic of the Tolerance measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The distribution of tilt preferences was not significantly different from uniform at 37, 57, and 97 cm.
source: Consistent with the previous result, the distribution of tilt preferences was not significantly different from uniform at any distance (χ2; 37, 57, and 97 cm: p≥0.43; 137 cm: p=0.03, not significant after Bonferroni-Holm correction; Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of orientation preferences shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The distribution of slant preferences at 57 cm (fixation distance) was not significantly different from uniform.
source: Likewise, the distribution of slant preferences at 57 cm (fixation distance) was not significantly different from uniform (p=0.13).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of orientation preferences.

claim: The distributions of slant preferences were significantly different from uniform at 37, 97, and 137 cm.
source: However, the distributions of slant preferences were significantly different from uniform at 37, 97, and 137 cm (all p≤1.2x10−3 and Bonferroni-Holm corrected).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of orientation preferences.

claim: At distances away from fixation, the mean slant preference across the population was larger than at 57 cm.
source: At each of these distances, the mean slant preference across the population was larger than at 57 cm.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of slant preferences at different distances.

claim: The slant preferences of individual neurons tended to increase between 57 and 97 cm.
source: Indeed, the preferences tended to increase between 57 and 97 cm (mean ΔSlant = 5.3°; paired t-test, p=1.1×10−3, N = 144 tuned at both distances)
evidence: This is supported by within-neuron analysis of slant preferences.

claim: The slant preferences of individual neurons tended to increase between 97 and 137 cm.
source: as well as between 97 and 137 cm (mean ΔSlant = 4.3°; p=9.7×10−3, N = 87 tuned at both distances).
evidence: This is supported by within-neuron analysis of slant preferences.

claim: The behavioral tilt sensitivities and TDI values were highly correlated across all sixteen slant–distance combinations.
source: Indeed, across all sixteen slant–distance combinations, the tilt sensitivities and TDI values were highly correlated (Monkey L: r = 0.95, p=2.2×10−308; Monkey F: r = 0.93, p=2.2×10−308).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of behavioral and neuronal data.

claim: The 3D tilt sensitivity of the monkeys was closely related to the tilt discriminability of CIP neurons over a wide range of viewing conditions.
source: Thus, the 3D tilt sensitivity of the monkeys was closely related to the tilt discriminability of CIP neurons over a wide range of viewing conditions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the high correlation between behavioral sensitivity and neuronal TDI values.

claim: Tilt sensitivity increased as a function of response amplitude.
source: Consistent with the prediction, tilt sensitivity increased as a function of response amplitude (Monkey L: Spearman r = 0.95, p=2.2×10−308; Monkey F: r = 0.87, p=2.2×10−308).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: CIP activity may constrain the precision of tilt perception.
source: The finding that the neuronal responses predicted behavioral sensitivity across performance levels ranging from near-chance to near-perfect suggests that CIP activity may constrain the precision of tilt perception.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the relationship between neuronal responses and behavioral sensitivity.

claim: 201 neurons (46%) had significant choice-related activity.
source: Across the population, 201 neurons (46%) had significant choice-related activity (ANOVA, p<0.05).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of choice responses.

claim: The choice tuning curves were well described by von Mises functions (mean r = 0.88 ± 0.10 Std Dev).
source: Across the population, the choice tuning curves were well described by von Mises functions (mean r = 0.88 ± 0.10 Std Dev, N = 201).
evidence: This is supported by fitting analysis of choice tuning curves.

claim: The median circular difference between principal surface tilt and choice preferences was −8.3° and not significantly different from 0°.
source: The median circular difference between the preferences was −8.3° and not significantly different from 0° (circular median test, p=0.24; N = 166 neurons with orientation and choice tuning), indicating that the sensory and choice preferences generally aligned.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of preference alignment.

claim: The alignment of preferred surface tilts and choice report directions reflected the task training.
source: Importantly, we found that the alignment was reversed in the two data sets (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with a previous study shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The association between 3D orientation selectivity and choice report directions was flexible and experience dependent.
source: This comparison indicates that the association between 3D orientation selectivity and choice report directions did not simply reflect a natural correspondence but was instead flexible and experience dependent.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of results from monkeys trained on opposite tasks.

claim: More neurons showed significant orientation tuning at each distance in the SPC window than the SD window.
source: In particular, more neurons showed significant orientation tuning at each distance in the SPC window than the SD window (ANOVA, p<0.05; Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The neurons tended to have orientation tuning at more distances in the SPC window than the SD window.
source: Correspondingly, the neurons tended to have orientation tuning at more distances in the SPC window than the SD window (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: There was a reduction in the number of neurons which were distance but not orientation selective in the SPC window (N = 20, 5%) compared to the SD window (N = 62, 14%).
source: There was also a reduction in the number of neurons which were distance but not orientation selective in the SPC window (two-way ANOVA; N = 20, 5%) compared to the SD window (N = 62, 14%).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of neuronal selectivity.

claim: The mean SPC window Tolerance (0.66 ± 0.16 Std Dev) was greater than the mean SD window Tolerance (0.58 ± 0.15 Std Dev), and the difference was statistically significant.
source: Consistent with a shift towards a higher-level 3D pose representation, the mean SPC window Tolerance (0.66 ± 0.16 Std Dev, N = 437) was greater than the mean SD window Tolerance (0.58 ± 0.15 Std Dev), and the difference was statistically significant (paired t-test, p=1.3×10−18; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Neurons with choice-related activity had a higher mean Tolerance (0.61) in the SD window than those without choice-related activity (0.56), and the difference was statistically significant.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, neurons with choice-related activity had a higher mean Tolerance (0.61) than those without choice-related activity (0.56), and the difference was statistically significant (ANOVA followed by Tukey's HSD test, p=0.02).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The number of neurons with slant tuning was 334 (76%) in the SD window and 370 (85%) in the SPC window.
source: The number of neurons with slant tuning was 334 (76%) in the SD window and 370 (85%) in the SPC window.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of neuronal selectivity.

claim: The number of neurons with distance tuning was 414 (95%) in the SD window and 412 (94%) in the SPC window.
source: The number of neurons with distance tuning was 414 (95%) in the SD window and 412 (94%) in the SPC window.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of neuronal selectivity.

claim: The mean Tolerance values between neurons with (0.72) and without (0.60) choice-related activity in the SPC window were significantly different.
source: First, we compared the mean Tolerance values between neurons with (0.72) and without (0.60) choice-related activity in the SPC window and found that the difference was statistically significant (ANOVA followed by Tukey's HSD test, p=3.8×10−9; Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The Tolerance values significantly increased for neurons with choice-related activity between the SD and SPC windows.
source: Indeed, the Tolerance values significantly increased for neurons with choice-related activity (p=3.8×10−9; Figure 7C)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The Tolerance values did not significantly increase for neurons without choice-related activity between the SD and SPC windows.
source: but not neurons without choice-related activity (p=0.06).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: For neurons with choice-related activity, the SPC window Tolerance was significantly correlated with the strength of choice-related activity.
source: For neurons with choice-related activity, we additionally found that the SPC window Tolerance was significantly correlated with the strength of choice-related activity (log of the choice tuning curve amplitude): r = 0.45, p=2.8×10−11.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis.

claim: The mean deviation in orientation preferences was greater in the SD (28.3°) than the SPC (20.4°) window.
source: The mean deviation was greater in the SD (28.3°) than the SPC (20.4°) window and the cumulative density functions were significantly different between the time windows (Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, p=1.4x10−10).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 7F.

claim: The orientation preferences of individual neurons were more similar across distance after the onset of choice-related activity than before.
source: Thus, the orientation preferences of individual neurons were more similar across distance after the onset of choice-related activity than before.
evidence: This is an inference based on the analysis of angular deviations in orientation preferences.

claim: CIP carries motor-related activity.
source: Importantly, the visually guided saccade task revealed that CIP carries motor-related activity.
evidence: This is supported by data showing saccade direction selectivity in CIP neurons.

claim: Saccade direction selectivity started 102 ms before the saccade onset.
source: Saccade direction selectivity started 102 ms before the saccade onset (ANOVA, p<0.05).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of saccade-related activity time courses shown in Figure 8B.

claim: 274 neurons (63%) had significant saccade direction tuning.
source: Across the population, 274 neurons (63%) had significant saccade direction tuning (ANOVA, p<0.05).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of saccade responses.

claim: The saccade direction tuning curves were well described by von Mises functions (mean r = 0.91 ± 0.10 Std Dev).
source: The tuning curves were well described by von Mises functions (mean r = 0.91 ± 0.10 Std Dev, N = 274).
evidence: This is supported by fitting analysis of saccade direction tuning curves.

claim: For neurons with choice-related activity, the median circular difference between principal surface tilt and saccade direction preferences was −1.6° and not significantly different from 0°.
source: For neurons with (without) choice-related activity, the median circular difference between preferences was −1.6° (−0.9°), and not significantly different from 0° (circular median test, both p≥0.61).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 9A.

claim: For neurons without choice-related activity, the median circular difference between principal surface tilt and saccade direction preferences was −0.9° and not significantly different from 0°.
source: For neurons with (without) choice-related activity, the median circular difference between preferences was −1.6° (−0.9°), and not significantly different from 0° (circular median test, both p≥0.61).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 9B.

claim: The distribution of preference differences between surface tilt and saccade direction was significantly narrower for neurons with choice-related activity than without.
source: Although the tilt and saccade direction preferences generally aligned regardless of choice-related activity, the distribution of preference differences was significantly narrower for neurons with (circular variance = 0.36) than without (circular variance = 0.74) choice-related activity (two-sample concentration difference test, p=3.2×10−5; Fisher, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: 137 neurons (31%) had both choice- and saccade-related activity.
source: Across the population, 137 neurons (31%) had both choice- and saccade-related activity.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of neuronal functional properties.

claim: For neurons with both choice- and saccade-related activity, the median circular difference between choice and saccade direction preferences was 2.9° and not significantly different from 0°.
source: For these neurons, the choice and saccade direction preferences generally aligned (Figure 9C). The median circular difference between the preferences was 2.9° and not significantly different from 0° (circular median test, p=0.61).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 9C.

claim: The choice tuning curves were systematically broader than the saccade direction tuning curves.
source: Supporting this distinction, the choice tuning curves were systematically broader than the saccade direction tuning curves (average ∆HWHH = 12°; within-neuron comparison, N = 137), and the difference was statistically significant (sign tests on the von Mises κ's and HWHHs, both p≤4.0x10−6).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of tuning curve properties.

claim: Many neurons had saccade-related activity only (137, 31%) or choice-related activity only (64, 15%).
source: We also found that many neurons had saccade-related activity only (137, 31%) or choice-related activity only (64, 15%), indicating that these properties were dissociable across the population (Figure 9D).
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 9D.

claim: Choice- and saccade-related activities were associated but functionally distinct.
source: Together, these results suggest that choice- and saccade-related activities were associated but functionally distinct.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differences in tuning properties and dissociability across the population.

claim: For neurons with choice-related activity, the Tolerance values of subpopulations with and without saccade-related activity were not significantly different in either time window.
source: The Tolerance values of these subpopulations were not significantly different in either time window (ANOVA followed by Tukey's HSD test, both p≥0.14; Figure 10A,B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 10A,B.

claim: For neurons with choice-related activity, the robustness of 3D selectivity was not associated with saccade-related activity.
source: Thus, for neurons with choice-related activity, the robustness of 3D selectivity was not associated with saccade-related activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of significant differences in Tolerance values.

claim: Choice-related activity was sufficient for the robustness of 3D selectivity to increase across the time windows.
source: Thus, choice-related activity was sufficient for the robustness of 3D selectivity to increase across the time windows and saccade-related activity was not necessary.
evidence: This is an inference based on the analysis of subpopulations with and without saccade-related activity.

claim: For neurons without choice-related activity, saccade-related activity was not associated with more robust 3D selectivity.
source: Thus, for neurons without choice-related activity, saccade-related activity was not associated with more robust 3D selectivity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the analysis of subpopulations with and without saccade-related activity.

claim: Choice-related activity was necessary for the robustness of 3D selectivity to increase across the time windows.
source: Thus, choice-related activity was necessary for the robustness of 3D selectivity to increase across the time windows and saccade-related activity was not sufficient.
evidence: This is an inference based on the analysis of subpopulations with and without choice-related activity.

claim: The robustness of 3D visual representations was linked to choice-related activity but not saccade-related activity.
source: These results further support that choice- and saccade-related activities were functionally distinct and suggest that the robustness of 3D visual representations was linked to choice-related activity but not saccade-related activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the analysis of subpopulations.

claim: CIP was only recently confirmed to be an architectonically distinct brain region.
source: In this study, we investigated the relationships between the robustness of 3D visual representations, choice-related activity, and motor-related activity in area CIP, a relatively understudied region of parietal cortex that was only recently confirmed to be an architectonically distinct brain region (Katsuyama et al., 2010; Niu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Transforming 2D retinal images into 3D visual representations is a nonlinear optimization problem.
source: Transforming 2D retinal images into 3D visual representations is a nonlinear optimization problem (Hartley and Zisserman, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Neurons in CIP achieve 3D orientation selectivity through the integration of stereoscopic and perspective cues.
source: Neurons in CIP achieve 3D orientation selectivity through the integration of stereoscopic and perspective cues (Tsutsui et al., 2001; Tsutsui et al., 2002; Rosenberg and Angelaki, 2014b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The orientation selectivity of many CIP neurons was highly tolerant to distance.
source: We found that the orientation selectivity of many CIP neurons was highly tolerant to distance.
evidence: This is supported by the Tolerance measurements presented in the study.

claim: The vast majority of neurons had significant distance tuning.
source: Importantly, that tolerance did not simply reflect selectivity for perspective cues (which were independent of distance) since the vast majority of neurons also had significant distance tuning.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of neuronal selectivity.

claim: Representations of 3D object pose based on relative disparities are created hierarchically, beginning with V1 neurons that represent local absolute binocular disparities.
source: Functional properties and connectivity data suggest that representations of 3D object pose based on relative disparities are created hierarchically, beginning with V1 neurons that represent local absolute binocular disparities (Cumming and Parker, 1997; Cumming and Parker, 1999; Cumming and Parker, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: A transformation towards relative disparity tuning proceeds in V2.
source: A transformation towards relative disparity tuning proceeds in V2 (Thomas et al., 2002)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: In V3A, absolute disparity representations may still predominate but selectivity for disparity gradients may also begin.
source: and V3A where absolute disparity representations may still predominate (Anzai et al., 2011) but selectivity for disparity gradients may also begin (Elmore et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The 2D-to-3D transformation likely progresses further in the posterior intraparietal area where tuning for local relative disparity gradients may be solidified.
source: The 2D-to-3D transformation likely progresses further in the posterior intraparietal area where tuning for local relative disparity gradients may be solidified (Alizadeh et al., 2018), ultimately achieving 3D object pose selectivity in CIP.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on previous research.

claim: The slant preferences of individual neurons tended to increase with distance behind fixation.
source: We found that the slant preferences of individual neurons tended to increase with distance behind fixation.
evidence: This is supported by within-neuron analysis of slant preferences.

claim: The increase in slant preferences with distance indicates that orientation and distance tuning was not strictly separable.
source: Although the increase was relatively small, it indicates that orientation and distance tuning was not strictly separable.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed changes in slant preferences with distance.

claim: Tilt sensitivity fell off more gradually with distance from fixation at larger compared to smaller slants.
source: Importantly, this finding was consistent with the behavioral data which showed that tilt sensitivity fell off more gradually with distance from fixation at larger compared to smaller slants
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data presented in the study.

claim: Following the onset of choice-related activity there was no attenuation in selectivity for slant or distance across the population.
source: Following the onset of choice-related activity there was no attenuation in selectivity for slant or distance across the population.
evidence: This is supported by analysis showing that the number of neurons with slant and distance tuning did not decrease in the SPC window.

claim: The low-dimensional task did not reduce the number of features maintained in the neuronal representation of the multi-dimensional stimulus.
source: Thus, the low-dimensional task ('report the tilt') did not reduce the number of features maintained in the neuronal representation of the multi-dimensional (tilt, slant, and distance) stimulus.
evidence: This is an inference based on the persistence of slant and distance tuning.

claim: For neurons with choice-related activity, the robustness of 3D selectivity increased across the SD and SPC windows.
source: Instead, for neurons with choice-related activity, the robustness of 3D selectivity increased across the SD and SPC windows.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of Tolerance values across time windows.

claim: The increased fidelity of the 3D representations may enable more robust perception and flexible sensorimotor processing.
source: Importantly, the increased fidelity of the 3D representations may enable more robust perception and flexible sensorimotor processing.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Choice-related activity is traditionally associated with feedforward contributions to perception.
source: Choice-related activity is traditionally associated with feedforward contributions to perception (Celebrini and Newsome, 1994; Britten et al., 1996; Dodd et al., 2001; Nienborg and Cumming, 2006; Gu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Existing measures of choice-related activity likely reflect combinations of feedforward contributions, attentional effects, and correlated activity.
source: Indeed, existing measures of choice-related activity likely reflect combinations of these factors (Haefner et al., 2013; Gu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Surface tilt and choice preferences typically aligned, consistent with a feedforward origin of choice-related activity.
source: We found that surface tilt and choice preferences typically aligned, consistent with a feedforward origin of choice-related activity and contrasting with the potentially non-specific effects of a feedback origin, as thought to occur in the ventral intraparietal area (Zaidel et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference based on the alignment of preferences and comparison with other brain areas.

claim: Neurons with more robust tuning for task-relevant information may have greater weight in the neural readout.
source: Thus, a potential implication of the current findings is that neurons with more robust tuning for task-relevant information have greater weight in the neural readout.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: The association between 3D visual orientation and choice report directions was flexible.
source: Importantly, this collective finding indicates that the association between 3D visual orientation and choice report directions did not simply reflect a natural correspondence. Instead, it was flexible, reflecting an experience-dependent association between perception and action.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with a previous study.

claim: CIP activity correlated with the direction and timing of visually guided saccades.
source: Specifically, CIP activity correlated with the direction and timing of visually guided saccades, implicating the area in visuomotor control for the first time.
evidence: This is supported by data from the visually guided saccade task.

claim: There was a sensorimotor association between the surface tilt and saccade direction preferences.
source: Moreover, there was a sensorimotor association between the surface tilt and saccade direction preferences, indicating that visual and oculomotor activities were not simply multiplexed.
evidence: This is supported by data showing alignment of preferences.

claim: The choice-related activity did not simply reflect saccade preparation signals.
source: These findings suggest that the choice-related activity did not simply reflect saccade preparation signals.
evidence: This is an inference based on the dissociation of choice- and saccade-related activities.

claim: Neurons with robust 3D selectivity and strong sensorimotor associations may have the greatest weight in determining motor responses.
source: Thus, a potential implication of the current findings is that neurons with robust 3D selectivity and strong sensorimotor associations have the greatest weight in determining motor responses.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Associating robust sensory and motor-related activity at the single neuron level may help ensure successful and timely interactions with the environment.
source: Indeed, associating robust sensory and motor-related activity at the single neuron level may help ensure successful and timely interactions with the environment since the same neurons represent the relevant sensory information and signal the appropriate motor response.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Experience has ongoing effects on the functional properties of CIP neurons.
source: Lastly, our findings reveal that experience has ongoing effects on the functional properties of CIP neurons, as occurs in downstream area LIP (Freedman and Assad, 2006; Law and Gold, 2008; Bennur and Gold, 2011), producing flexible mappings between sensory, choice-, and motor-related activity that support goal-directed behaviors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experience-dependent associations found in the study and comparison with other brain areas.

claim: Two male rhesus monkeys were used in the study.
source: Two male rhesus monkeys (Macaca mulatta; Monkey L: 6 years of age, ~9.5 kg; Monkey F: 5 years, ~6.4 kg) were surgically implanted with a Delrin ring for head restraint and a removable recording grid for guiding electrodes (Rosenberg et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes the experimental subjects.

claim: Stimuli were rear-projected onto a polarization preserving screen using a DLP LED projector with 1280 × 720 pixel resolution at 240 Hz.
source: They were rear-projected onto a polarization preserving screen (Stewart Film Screen, Inc) using a DLP LED projector (PROPixx; VPixx Technologies, Inc) with 1280 × 720 pixel resolution (70° × 43°) at 240 Hz (120 Hz/eye).
evidence: This describes the experimental apparatus.

claim: The stimuli consisted of 250 nonoverlapping dots uniformly distributed across a plane.
source: They consisted of 250 nonoverlapping dots uniformly distributed across a plane.
evidence: This describes the stimulus properties.

claim: Recordings were performed using silicone linear array probes with either four or eight tetrodes.
source: Recordings were performed using silicone linear array probes with either four or eight tetrodes (NeuroNexus, Inc).
evidence: This describes the recording methods.

claim: 218 neurons were recorded from the left hemisphere of Monkey L.
source: Only well-isolated single neurons verified by at least two authors were included for analysis: 218 neurons from the left hemisphere of Monkey L (26 sessions) and 219 neurons from the right hemisphere of Monkey F (27 sessions).
evidence: This describes the data collection.

claim: 219 neurons were recorded from the right hemisphere of Monkey F.
source: Only well-isolated single neurons verified by at least two authors were included for analysis: 218 neurons from the left hemisphere of Monkey L (26 sessions) and 219 neurons from the right hemisphere of Monkey F (27 sessions).
evidence: This describes the data collection.
